articles.title: Classify Text Data Using an Embeddings API in Node.js: Portable Invoice Field Decisions
articles.excerpt: Short answer: To classify invoice text data using embeddings in Node.js, compare snippets with application-owned field prototypes, keep an unknown result, and isolate the provider behind a batch adapt…
articles.body: Short answer: To classify invoice text data using embeddings in Node.js, compare snippets with application-owned field prototypes, keep an unknown result, and isolate the provider behind a batch adapter so the taxonomy survives an API change. The practical way to classify text data using embeddings in Node.js is to keep the label decision in your application and treat the embeddings API as a replaceable vector service. For a B2B SaaS product extracting fields from supplier invoices, that means embedding OCR text, comparing it with versioned field examples, and rejecting uncertain matches before a value reaches an accounting workflow. The provider should return a vector; it should not own your taxonomy. That boundary matters. The index is disposable.

articles.excerpt: AI startups expanding overseas tend to focus on localization, pricing and growth channels. Security often gets one line in the launch plan. That's risky: once an AI product is in front of a global aud…
articles.body: AI startups expanding overseas tend to focus on localization, pricing and growth channels. Security often gets one line in the launch plan. That's risky: once an AI product is in front of a global audience, people will try to extract its system prompt, push it into off-policy answers, or abuse connected tools. A single viral screenshot of your assistant leaking internal instructions or customer data can undo months of marketing. Here is a practical checklist to run before launch. 1. System prompt hygiene Assume the system prompt will leak. Don't put secrets, API keys, internal URLs or confidential pricing logic in it. Keep instructions short and specific. Long, contradictory prompts are easier to manipulate. Separate policy from persona.

articles.title: How to structure Stripe, Mercado Pago, and Asaas in one Laravel codebase
articles.excerpt: If you're building a SaaS for the Latin American market, you will inevitably face a hard architectural decision: how do you support multiple payment providers without turning your codebase into a mess…
articles.body: If you're building a SaaS for the Latin American market, you will inevitably face a hard architectural decision: how do you support multiple payment providers without turning your codebase into a mess of if/else statements? You might start with Stripe, since it's the standard for international recurring billing. Then a client asks for PIX, and you need Mercado Pago. Another client wants boleto bancário , and now you need Asaas. If you're not careful, your PaymentController turns into a 500-line monster full of provider-specific logic. Here's the architecture I use to solve this: the Driver/Adapter pattern with a typed interface . The Core Idea The goal is simple: your domain depends on a single contract, and each provider is just a new class.

articles.title: Analog astronauts: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.excerpt: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.body: I have been dreaming of doing research in space as an astronaut my whole life, but for some reason, the thought of working underwater made me nervous. I’ve known for a long time that astronauts train underwater to simulate different scenarios they’re likely to experience in space. Diving was never an issue for me, either — I even made it as far as becoming a certified rescue diver. So what was the problem? This summer, I led a simulated space mission in an underwater habitat called the Jules’ Undersea Lab. It is a research station that is located 22 feet (6.7 meters) underwater near Key Largo, Florida. You have to scuba dive to get in and out of the station. To become an aquanaut , you have to stay underwater for at least 24 hours in a so-called state of saturation.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 26, 2004: Cassini spacecraft takes 1st-ever closeup photos of Saturn moon Titan
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 26, 2004, NASA's Cassini spacecraft took the first close-up images of Saturn's largest moon Titan. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 26, 2004, NASA's Cassini spacecraft took the first close-up images of Saturn's largest moon Titan. The Cassini spacecraft would later drop off a probe on Titan named Huygens, which was a European spacecraft that hitched a ride to the Saturn system with the Cassini mission. But before Cassini dropped off its robotic passenger, it flew by Titan a few times and took some amazing photos . Cassini completed its first flyby on July 3, 2004, but when it swung by a second time on Oct. 26, it got about 300 times closer than it did the first time. At the closest point of this flyby, Cassini was 745 miles (1,200 kilometers) away from the surface of Titan. The spacecraft took hundreds of photos during this flyby , and these were the highest resolution views of Titan anyone had ever seen.

articles.title: NASA ends Swift space telescope mission after failed rescue attempt
articles.excerpt: NASA has officially ended the mission of its Swift Observatory, after a private satellite failed to meet up with the aging spacecraft in orbit.
articles.body: NASA has officially ended the mission of its Swift space telescope, after a private satellite failed in its bold bid to rescue the aging spacecraft. That rescue mission was led by the Arizona company Katalyst Space Technologies, whose LINK spacecraft tried to meet up with Swift this summer to boost its orbit. That didn't work out, however, so Swift continues its fall back toward Earth. The telescope is expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere "in the next few weeks," NASA said in a statement on Friday (Oct. 23). That statement served primarily to announce the end of the Swift mission after more than 20 very productive years. The telescope launched to Earth orbit in November 2004, tasked with studying gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) — the most powerful explosions in the cosmos.

The term "cult classic" has been loosely bandied about in cinematic circles until its definition has diluted into nothingness, but never has it been more appropriately applied than to director Richard Kelly’s strange psychological sci-fi thriller, "Donnie Darko", which celebrates its milestone 25th birthday today. Starring Jake Gyllenhaal, Drew Barrymore, Mary McDonnell, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Patrick Swayze, Jena Malone, and Noah Wyle, "Donnie Darko" was released on Oct. 26, 2001, into an unstable world still shocked by the catastrophic Sept. 11 terrorist attacks less than two months earlier.
